text:
The Long Way Home

On the afternoon of April 11, 1970, a Saturn V rocket lifted from Cape Kennedy carrying three men toward the Moon. Apollo 13 was meant to be the third lunar landing, and by then the public had grown casual about the whole enterprise. Networks had not even bothered to broadcast the crew's early television transmissions. That indifference would not last the week.

The commander was Jim Lovell, a veteran of three earlier flights who was about to become the first person to fly to the Moon twice. Fred Haise, a rookie, was to pilot the lunar module. The third seat should have gone to Ken Mattingly, but a few days before launch doctors learned he had been exposed to German measles, and NASA replaced him with the backup command module pilot, Jack Swigert. Swigert had trained for only a few days as a prime crew member. Mattingly, grounded and frustrated, would later play a large part in saving the men who flew without him.

The crew named their command module Odyssey and their lunar lander Aquarius. For two days the flight went smoothly. On the evening of April 13, roughly 200,000 miles from home, Mission Control asked Swigert to flip a switch that stirred the supercold oxygen and hydrogen stored in tanks in the service module. These tanks fed the fuel cells that made the spacecraft's electricity and drinking water, and the oxygen supplied the cabin air.

The stirring was routine. This time it set off a catastrophe. Years earlier, an oxygen tank had been dropped slightly during handling. Later, during a ground test, its heater had run far too hot and stripped the insulation from the wiring inside. When Swigert threw the switch, a spark in that bare wiring ignited the oxygen. Tank number two ruptured, and the blast blew a panel off the side of the service module and crippled the neighboring tank.

Inside the capsule, the crew felt a bang and a shudder. Swigert reported the trouble first, and Lovell followed with the understated line that has become famous, "Houston, we've had a problem." Warning lights multiplied. Voltage dropped. Haise looked out a window and saw gas streaming into space. Lovell understood what that meant. The oxygen was leaving, and the fuel cells that depended on it were dying.

At Mission Control in Houston, flight director Gene Kranz gathered his teams. The first question was how to get the ship home. The most direct route, an engine burn to turn around, would depend on the service module's main engine, and nobody could trust a spacecraft that had just exploded. Instead, controllers chose to let the Moon's gravity do the work. Apollo 13 would swing around the far side and be flung back toward Earth, with an engine burn after the pass to speed the return.

The next problem was where to live. Odyssey was losing power and would soon be dead, and its batteries had to be saved for the final minutes of reentry. The only refuge was Aquarius, still attached and fully working. But the lander was built to support two men for about two days on the lunar surface. Now it had to keep three men alive for four. Lovell and Haise moved into it, and Swigert shut down the command module piece by piece until it was a cold, silent shell.

The burn after the lunar flyby worked. Hours earlier the ship had passed about 160 miles above the far side of the Moon, and at its greatest distance it stood nearly 250,000 miles from Earth, farther than any humans have ever traveled. Lovell, Swigert and Haise could see the lunar landscape they had come to walk on, and none of them had time to enjoy it.

Then came the slow, grinding part. The crew had little water. Haise would develop a fever and a painful infection. Drinking was rationed to a few ounces a day, and the men ate sparingly. Without the electricity to run heaters, the cabin temperature sank to near freezing. Condensation beaded on the walls. The astronauts wore their flight suits and put on whatever extra clothing they could find, and they struggled to sleep, which left them tired just when they needed to be sharp.

A more urgent threat was the air itself. Exhaled carbon dioxide had to be scrubbed out by canisters of lithium hydroxide, and Aquarius carried only enough for two men for a short time. The command module had plenty of canisters, but they were square, and the lander's system needed round ones. As the carbon dioxide level climbed toward dangerous territory, engineers on the ground assembled a fix from the things the crew actually had aboard. They used plastic bags, cardboard from a flight manual, a sock, and a great deal of duct tape. They read the instructions up to the crew, who built the contraption in space. The improvised adapter nicknamed the mailbox worked, and the carbon dioxide dropped.

Navigation raised another difficulty. Normally the spacecraft's guidance system would align itself using the stars, but the debris cloud from the explosion glittered around the ship and confused the sensors. The crew used the sunlit edge of the Earth as a reference and performed a course correction by hand. A single small burn done accurately mattered, because a slightly wrong angle could have let the capsule skip off the atmosphere or burn up in it.

Meanwhile, on the ground, Mattingly and a team of engineers worked in a simulator to devise a way to restart Odyssey after days of dormancy. The ship had never been designed to be switched back on from a cold state with such limited battery power. They wrote a procedure, tested it repeatedly, and rewrote it until it fit within what the batteries could give. Mattingly, who had never contracted the measles, now worked toward a goal that depended on his knowing the machine better than anyone.

On April 17, as Earth grew large in the windows, the crew began the final sequence. They released the damaged service module first. When it drifted away, they got a clear look at the wound. A whole side panel was missing, and the interior was a wreck. Lovell described it to Houston with obvious shock. Then the three men moved back into Odyssey, powered it up using the new procedure, and finally cast off Aquarius, which had served as their lifeboat and which would burn up in the atmosphere.

Reentry meant a communications blackout. Normally it lasts about three minutes, but this time it dragged on, and the silence in Mission Control grew heavy. Controllers had no idea whether the heat shield, which had endured days in the cold, had survived. Then, after a pause longer than anyone wanted, Swigert's voice came through. Odyssey's parachutes bloomed, and the capsule settled into the South Pacific near Samoa just after noon, within sight of the recovery ship.

The three men were weary, thin and cold, and they were alive. The mission had failed in its purpose, since no one landed on the Moon, yet it became one of the great demonstrations of what skilled people can do under pressure. The investigation that followed redesigned the oxygen tanks and their wiring. The astronauts, the controllers, and the engineers who had improvised a solution out of tape and cardboard had turned a disaster into a return, and the world, which had barely noticed the launch, watched the splashdown with relief.
